units.title: Discovery of (4-Pyrazolyl)-2-aminopyrimidines as Potent and Selective Inhibitors of Cyclin-Dependent Kinase 2
units.text: A screening hit that was really a JAK2 inhibitor, turned into a CDK2 inhibitor selective over five other CDKs.

units.title: The disease
units.text: CCNE1-amplified cancers, where cyclin E1 amplification drives proliferation and predicts poor prognosis, and where CDK2 activity is also a route of resistance to CDK4/6 inhibitors.

units.title: The selectivity problem
units.text: CDK1 is pan-lethal, so inhibiting it is thought to account for much of the toxicity of earlier multi-targeted CDK inhibitors. The campaign needed CDK2 potency with a wide margin over CDK1, and over CDK4, CDK6, CDK7 and CDK9. The screening hit also had to be stripped of its original JAK2 activity.

units.title: The property problem
units.text: Potency was never the hard part once the scaffold was found. Gastric solubility, human microsomal clearance and permeability were, and they moved against each other at every step.

units.title: A screening hit that preferred a different kinase
units.text: Screening an internal collection returned compound 1: submicromolar against CDK2 at 607 nM, but subnanomolar against JAK2, which was its real target. The pyrazolyl aminopyrimidine core was worth keeping. The anilino methanesulfonamide was not, because that end of the molecule sits in the hinge region, and hinge substitution is what decides kinase selectivity in this scaffold class. Ebvaciclib, carrying an aminopiperidine there, spares JAK2; zotiraciclib, carrying a substituted phenyl, inhibits both. So the hinge was the first thing to change.

units.title: A screening hit that preferred a different kinase
units.text: The starting molecule came out of testing a large library of compounds. It blocked the intended target, CDK2, only weakly, and blocked a different enzyme called JAK2 six hundred times more strongly. Its central shape was still promising, so the chemists kept that and replaced the flat end. That end sits in a part of the protein known to decide which enzymes a molecule will block, which made it the obvious place to start.

units.title: A three-dimensional ring erased JAK2 and found CDK2
units.text: Replacing the flat aniline with an sp3 1-(methylsulfonyl)piperidin-4-ylamine moved CDK2 potency from 607 nM to 16 nM and removed JAK2 activity entirely, past 10,000 nM. Selectivity against an in-house panel of eight kinases was clean. The authors attribute this to the sp3 hybridisation at the hinge rather than to any single new contact, and the later crystal structure shows why the group is tolerated: its sulfonamide oxygens reach the backbone amide of Asp86, with a water-mediated contact onward to Gln85 and Lys89.

units.title: A three-dimensional ring erased JAK2 and found CDK2
units.text: Swapping that flat end for a puckered, three-dimensional ring changed which protein the molecule cared about. It became nearly forty times better at CDK2, and it stopped blocking JAK2 altogether. It also left eight other enzymes alone. The reason is partly shape: a ring that is not flat fits this pocket without clashing, and the crystal structure later showed it making a firm grip on the protein's backbone.

units.title: Chlorine to trifluoromethyl, and CDK1 falls away
units.text: CDK1 was the isoform that mattered: it is pan-lethal, and much of the toxicity of earlier multi-targeted CDK inhibitors is thought to follow from inhibiting it. Compound 2 had only 64-fold margin. Exchanging the pyrimidine C5 chlorine for a trifluoromethyl group, which projects at the Phe80 gatekeeper, took CDK2 to 3.2 nM and CDK1 to 407 nM: 130-fold. That established C5 as the selectivity lever for the entire series, and the campaign returned to it three more times.

units.title: Chlorine to trifluoromethyl, and CDK1 falls away
units.text: The dangerous relative here is CDK1, which healthy cells cannot do without. The new molecule was only sixty-four times more selective for CDK2, which is not enough. Replacing one chlorine atom with a slightly bulkier fluorinated group doubled that margin and made the compound five times more potent. The change sits directly against a large residue that guards the entrance to the pocket, and it became the campaign's most reliable adjustment.

units.title: Solubility against selectivity, traded twelve times over
units.text: What follows in Tables 1 and 2 is not an optimisation so much as a negotiation. An isoelectronic N-methylpiperidine cleared 400 ug/mL of gastric solubility and dropped CDK1 margin from 130-fold to 29-fold. A nitrile lowered clearance and took solubility below 1 ug/mL. The one clean move was a nitrogen walk from N-methylpyrazole to N-methylimidazole on the sulfonyl group, which raised solubility from below 1 ug/mL to 322 ug/mL and cost nothing. Applying the C5 nitrile to that compound then undid the solubility again.

units.title: Solubility against selectivity, traded twelve times over
units.text: From here the work becomes a series of trades. Making the compound dissolve better usually made it less selective, and making it more selective usually made it dissolve worse. One change was free: moving a single nitrogen atom around a small ring made the compound more than three hundred times more soluble and made nothing else worse. The next attempt to improve it undid that gain, which is how this work usually goes.

units.title: Compound 17, and what it did in an animal
units.text: Compound 17 carries the trifluoromethyl at C5, the geminal dimethyl alcohol on the pyrazole and a cyclopropyl on the sulfonyl. It inhibits CDK2 at 0.29 nM with 220-fold margin over CDK1, dissolves above 400 ug/mL, clears at 0.5 L/h/kg and permeates well. In a panel of over fifty kinases, none was inhibited below 3 uM. In CCNE1-amplified OVCAR3 tumours it cut Rb phosphorylation by roughly half and gave 38 per cent tumour growth inhibition at 30 mg/kg. The crystal structure is 8UV0, at 1.55 A.

units.title: Compound 17, and what it did in an animal
units.text: The molecule they chose blocks CDK2 at a third of a nanomolar, leaves CDK1 alone more than two hundred times over, dissolves readily and survives the liver. Out of more than fifty other enzymes tested, it blocked none of them meaningfully. In mice carrying tumours of the type it was designed for, it halved the chemical signal that CDK2 produces and slowed tumour growth by about a third. Its crystal structure shows every contact the chemists had aimed for.

units.title: The swap that changed target
units.text: The anilino methanesulfonamide of the hit was replaced by an sp3 1-(methylsulfonyl)piperidin-4-ylamine at the pyrimidine C2 position. Precedent in this hinge region (ebvaciclib against zotiraciclib, and an aminopiperidine analogue of milciclib) associates sp3 hybridisation here with general kinase selectivity, and that is how the authors rationalise the result.

units.title: The swap that changed target
units.text: The starting molecule was really a JAK2 inhibitor. Replacing its flat aniline with a puckered, three-dimensional ring stopped it hitting JAK2 at all, and made it 38 times better at CDK2.

units.title: Chlorine to trifluoromethyl at the gatekeeper
units.text: Exchanging the C5 chloro for a trifluoromethyl fills the space against the Phe80 gatekeeper. CDK2 potency improved five-fold and CDK1 selectivity went from 64-fold to 130-fold, which established C5 as the isoform selectivity lever for the whole series.

units.title: Chlorine to trifluoromethyl at the gatekeeper
units.text: A small chlorine atom was swapped for a bulkier fluorinated group, right where the protein has a bulky residue of its own. This is the single change that separated CDK2 from its dangerous relative CDK1.

units.title: Tetrahydropyran to cyclohexyl
units.text: Replacing the tetrahydropyran oxygen with a plain methylene gives a lipophilic cyclohexyl. Potency and CDK1 selectivity survive, but simulated gastric fluid solubility falls to 11 ug/mL and human microsomal clearance rises to 1.1 L/h/kg.

units.title: Tetrahydropyran to cyclohexyl
units.text: Removing a single oxygen atom made the molecule greasier. It still worked on the enzyme, but it dissolved poorly and the liver cleared it quickly.

units.title: Isoelectronic swap to N-methylpiperidine
units.text: The cyclohexyl is exchanged for an isoelectronic 1-methylpiperidin-4-yl. Solubility clears 400 ug/mL and clearance falls to 0.7 L/h/kg, but CDK1 selectivity collapses from 130-fold to 29-fold and CDK6 potency drops to 153 nM.

units.title: Isoelectronic swap to N-methylpiperidine
units.text: Putting a nitrogen into the ring fixed the solubility problem immediately. The cost was severe: the molecule lost most of its margin over CDK1.

units.title: Saturated ring to ortho-fluorophenyl
units.text: Moving from a saturated ring to an ortho-fluorophenyl is tolerated in the enzyme assay at 2.1 nM with 170-fold CDK1 selectivity and clearance below 0.5 L/h/kg, but whole blood potency is poor at about 5 uM.

units.title: Saturated ring to ortho-fluorophenyl
units.text: An aromatic ring worked just as well against the purified enzyme, and the liver left it alone. In human blood, though, it barely worked at all: a warning that enzyme numbers are not the whole story.

units.title: Fluorine to chlorine
units.text: The ortho-fluorine becomes an ortho-chlorine. Enzyme potency improves nearly four-fold to 0.56 nM and whole blood potency improves six-fold to 823 nM, but human intrinsic clearance rises to 1 L/h/kg.

units.title: Fluorine to chlorine
units.text: Swapping fluorine for the larger chlorine made the molecule work far better in blood. The liver then cleared it faster, which is the problem the next few compounds try to solve.

units.title: Ring to 2,2,2-trifluoroethyl
units.text: Dropping the ring entirely for a short fluorinated chain keeps potency at 1.8 nM with 110-fold CDK1 selectivity and clearance below 0.5 L/h/kg, but solubility is only 3 ug/mL.

units.title: Ring to 2,2,2-trifluoroethyl
units.text: Replacing the ring with a small fluorinated tail kept the potency and the liver stability. It would barely dissolve, which is what the sulfonyl end of the molecule was then used to fix.

units.title: Fluorinated tail to geminal dimethyl alcohol
units.text: Exchanging the trifluoroethyl for a 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropyl group gives subnanomolar potency at 0.42 nM, 150-fold CDK1 selectivity, solubility of 842 ug/mL and clearance below 0.5 L/h/kg, at the cost of CDK6 potency at 160 nM.

units.title: Fluorinated tail to geminal dimethyl alcohol
units.text: Adding an alcohol group made the compound dissolve nearly three hundred times better and pushed potency below one nanomolar. This is the branch that eventually produced the lead.

units.title: A nitrile to slow the liver down
units.text: A cyano group at the para position of the 2-chlorophenyl lowers lipophilicity to cut intrinsic clearance to 0.5 L/h/kg while holding potency at 0.3 nM, but gastric solubility falls below 1 ug/mL.

units.title: A nitrile to slow the liver down
units.text: Adding a small polar group stopped the liver clearing the compound so fast. Solubility got worse again: the two properties kept trading against each other.

units.title: An ionisable amine for solubility
units.text: The nitrile becomes an N-methyl benzylamine, which both breaks molecular planarity and adds an ionisable centre. Solubility rises to 94 ug/mL, but CDK1 selectivity falls to 81-fold and CDK7 to 62-fold.

units.title: An ionisable amine for solubility
units.text: A basic amine was added to help the compound dissolve, and it did. But it also narrowed the safety margin over CDK1 and CDK7.

units.title: Trifluoromethyl to nitrile
units.text: Returning to the C5 lever, the trifluoromethyl is replaced by a cyano group. CDK1 selectivity recovers to 290-fold, CDK7 to 790-fold, and solubility improves to 221 ug/mL. Free fraction rises to 33%, which is how the authors explain the good whole blood translation at 112 nM.

units.title: Trifluoromethyl to nitrile
units.text: Changing that one group again recovered the lost safety margins and improved solubility at the same time. It also made more of the drug available in blood rather than stuck to blood proteins.

units.title: Methyl sulfonyl to N-methylpyrazole
units.text: The methyl on the sulfonyl is replaced by a 1-methylpyrazol-4-yl. Potency, clearance and Caco-2 permeability are all good, but gastric solubility stays below 1 ug/mL, so the solubility problem is not at this position yet.

units.title: Methyl sulfonyl to N-methylpyrazole
units.text: Putting a small ring on the sulfonyl end kept everything good except the one thing they were trying to fix. The compound still would not dissolve.

units.title: The nitrogen walk that fixed solubility
units.text: Moving one ring nitrogen, from 1-methylpyrazol-4-yl to the more polar 1-methylimidazol-4-yl, raises gastric solubility from below 1 ug/mL to 322 ug/mL while holding the ADME profile and improving whole blood potency to 334 nM.

units.title: The nitrogen walk that fixed solubility
units.text: Moving a single nitrogen atom around the ring made the compound over three hundred times more soluble. Nothing else about it got worse. This is the cleanest single edit in the paper.

units.title: The C5 lever does not always help
units.text: Applying the C5 trifluoromethyl to nitrile change that worked for 12 improves CDK1 selectivity to 290-fold and CDK7 to 5600-fold, but solubility falls from 322 to 5 ug/mL, CDK4 and CDK6 margins narrow, and Caco-2 permeability drops to 0.6.

units.title: The C5 lever does not always help
units.text: The same trick that helped earlier backfired here: selectivity improved but the compound stopped dissolving and stopped crossing membranes. Context, not the group itself, decides the outcome.

units.title: Imidazole to 2-pyridyl
units.text: Swapping the methylimidazole for a 2-pyridyl restores Caco-2 permeability to 18 but drops gastric solubility below 1 ug/mL. The authors record this as the point at which balancing the two at R3 was abandoned for this series.

units.title: Imidazole to 2-pyridyl
units.text: Another ring swap traded solubility straight back for permeability. After this the chemists gave up on this branch and went back to compound 9.

units.title: The cyclopropyl that finished it
units.text: With the pyrazole alcohol of 9 fixed, a cyclopropyl on the sulfonyl gives 0.29 nM potency, 220-fold CDK1 selectivity, gastric solubility above 400 ug/mL, clearance of 0.5 L/h/kg and Caco-2 of 13. This is compound 17, the lead, and the ligand in 8UV0.

units.title: The cyclopropyl that finished it
units.text: A small three-carbon ring on the sulfonyl end was the last piece. Everything the chemists wanted was finally true at once, and this is the molecule they took forward.

units.title: The C5 lever fails a third time
units.text: Applying the nitrile once more halves potency to 0.65 nM and narrows CDK1 to 190-fold, CDK4 to 26-fold and CDK6 to 95-fold, with solubility down to 41 ug/mL. On this scaffold the trifluoromethyl is the better group, which closes the C5 question the campaign opened at compound 2.

units.title: The C5 lever fails a third time
units.text: Trying the same swap on the finished molecule made it worse in every way that mattered. The trifluoromethyl stayed.

units.title: 8UV0, CDK2
units.text: Compound 17 in the CDK2 ATP site at 1.55 A. The 2-aminopyrimidine makes the hinge contact, the C5 trifluoromethyl points at the Phe80 gatekeeper, and the sulfonamide oxygens accept from the Asp86 backbone amide with a water-mediated contact to Lys89 and Gln85.

units.title: 8UV0, CDK2
units.text: The lead compound sitting in the pocket where CDK2 would normally hold ATP. Every contact the chemists designed is visible here, which is how they knew why the molecule worked.

units.title: BUILD_SPEC 9.5 item 6: two values in one cell. Confirmed and handled
units.text: BUILD_SPEC 9.5 item 6: two values in one cell. Confirmed and handled. Table 1 has a single `CDK4/D1 CDK6/D3 (nM)` column holding two numbers, for example `3.2/10` for compound 4. It is **not** a value/fold pair: in Table 2 the same isoforms get separate columns and compound 4's neighbours read `5/17x`, which *is* value/fold. `table1.tsv` therefore splits the Table 1 column into `cdk4_d1_ic50` and `cdk6_d3_ic50`, and only `cdk1_b1_ic50` carries a fold in that table. Misreading this would silently invent a 10-fold CDK4 margin for compound 4 where the paper reports 3.2 nM and 10 nM absolute.

units.title: Table 1 has no fold columns for CDK4 or CDK6, Table 2 has them for every isoform
units.text: Table 1 has no fold columns for CDK4 or CDK6, Table 2 has them for every isoform. The published folds are carried across exactly as printed and are never recomputed, so a reader comparing the app with the paper sees the same numbers. Where a fold is absent it stays absent rather than being derived.

units.title: SMILES provenance, and how strongly each one is verified
units.text: SMILES provenance, and how strongly each one is verified. No structure was read off a table image. Compounds 2 to 18 were built from the IUPAC names in the Experimental Section. Every one matches the molecular formula the paper reports for its `(M + H)+`, and **sixteen of them (compounds 3 to 18) were additionally confirmed atom for atom** by parsing the published name with OPSIN and comparing canonical SMILES: all sixteen agree. That second check matters more than it sounds. While curating the FGFR bundle, a hand-built scaffold reproduced the published molecular formula **exactly while having the wrong connectivity**: an ether oxygen had migrated. A formula check cannot see that, and a depiction built from it would have been quietly wrong in every panel. Formula agreement is necessary and is not sufficient. Two compounds here rest on weaker evidence and are marked as such: - **Compound 2**: its name sits inside a "Step 2" heading rather than under its own compound heading, so it was verified by formula (C18H26ClN6O3S) rather than by name. - **Compound 1**: the HTS hit has no synthesis in the paper at all, and was transcribed by eye from the Figure 2 depiction. It is the one identity in this bundle resting on a drawing, and it is flagged in `compounds.tsv` `notes`. Compound 17 uses the RCSB chemical component `XKU` SMILES verbatim, so the depiction cannot drift from the crystal ligand.

units.title: Compound 1 is racemic
units.text: Compound 1 is racemic (published as `(+/-)-1`). The SMILES carries no stereocentre configuration, which is correct for a racemate, so any ligand efficiency or property calculation treats it as one species. ## Disagreements inside the paper, both readings kept

units.text: Compound 9 gastric solubility: text says `>400 ug/mL`, Table 1 says `842 ug/mL`. The table value is used for plotting because it is a measurement rather than a bound, and the text reading is recorded here. Same pattern, opposite direction, for compound 5, where the table itself prints `>400`: that one stays a bound with its qualifier preserved.

units.text: Compound 17 gastric solubility is `>400 ug/mL` in both text and Table 2. It is a bound, not a number, and must not be coerced to 400 in any plot or sort.

units.title: Compound 6 whole blood potency: text says `about 5 uM`, Table 1 says `5111 nM`
units.text: Compound 6 whole blood potency: text says `about 5 uM`, Table 1 says `5111 nM`. These agree; the table value is used. Noted only because the text rounds. ## What PLIP reproduces of the published structure description, and what it does not The paper describes four things about compound 17 in 8UV0. PLIP, run through the vendored `cif2plip` preparation, reproduces three of them outright: | Paper's claim | PLIP result | |---|---| | The 2-aminopyrimidine makes the hinge binding interaction | Two hydrogen bonds to Leu83, 1.85 A and 2.35 A | | Sulfonamide oxygens accept from the backbone N-H of Asp86 | Hydrogen bond to Asp86, 2.17 A, protein as donor | | The tertiary hydroxyl interacts with Asp145 | Hydrogen bond to Asp145, 2.71 A | | A water-mediated interaction with Lys89 **and** Gln85 | Partly: a water bridge to **Gln85** (2.98 A and 3.06 A legs), plus a **direct** hydrogen bond to Lys89 at 2.93 A |

units.title: The Lys89 contact is direct in PLIP's reading, water-mediated in the paper's
units.text: The Lys89 contact is direct in PLIP's reading, water-mediated in the paper's. Checked against the coordinates independently: water A491 sits within hydrogen-bonding distance of both Gln85 NE2 and Lys89 NZ, so the structural claim is sound and the difference is one of assignment, not of fact. Both readings are shown in the app: the contact list reports what PLIP measured, and the caption states what the authors described. Neither is presented as the other.

units.title: PLIP calls a salt bridge to Asp86 at 4.96 A
units.text: PLIP calls a salt bridge to Asp86 at 4.96 A. Compound 17 carries no formal charge at that end of the molecule (the piperidine nitrogen is sulfonylated, so it is not basic), which makes this assignment doubtful. It is kept because the pipeline does not edit PLIP's output, but it is worth knowing before the contact is built into any narrative.

units.title: The trifluoromethyl to Phe80 contact does not appear at all
units.text: The trifluoromethyl to Phe80 contact does not appear at all. This is the single most important interaction in the campaign's story and PLIP classifies nothing for it: the contact is a fluorine pointing at an aromatic face, which falls outside PLIP's hydrophobic and pi-stacking criteria. The Structure sheet must therefore draw the Phe80 relationship from the motif annotation and the paper's own description, not from the contact list, and must not imply a measured interaction where there is none. ## Open decisions for review

units.title: `change_type` enum extension
units.text: `change_type` enum extension. BUILD_SPEC 5.7 fixes the `change_type` vocabulary, but it has no term for *adding* a polar group to lower lipophilicity, which is what compounds 10, 11 and the alcohol of 9 do. `polarity_reduction` means the opposite. Three edits (`cdk2-e08`, `cdk2-e09`, `cdk2-e10`) use **`polar_addition`**, an addition to the enum. The alternative is to overload `bioisostere`, which would hide the campaign's most repeated property move. Flagged for Marc.

units.title: OVCAR3 pNPM T199 direction is inverted relative to every other potency column
units.text: OVCAR3 pNPM T199 direction is inverted relative to every other potency column. It is a cellular CDK1 counter-screen, so a *higher* IC50 is the better result. `assays.json` marks it `direction: higher_better`. Any generic "lower is better" colour scale over potency columns would paint this one exactly wrong.

units.title: Table 3 doses differ row by row
units.text: Table 3 doses differ row by row (cassette against discrete, and three different oral doses). AUC values are not comparable across rows without the footnote, so each row carries its own `dose_note` and the Properties sheet must show it beside the PK ladder. ## Not applicable to this bundle 11. BUILD_SPEC 9.5 items 1 to 5 concern the JAK1, KRAS and FGFR bundles and are recorded in their own `ISSUES.md` files when those are curated in Stage 3.

units.title: Discovery of Potent and Selective Inhibitors of Wild-Type and Gatekeeper Mutant Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptor (FGFR) 2/3
units.text: An inhibitor that still works on the gatekeeper mutants that defeat the approved pan-FGFR drugs, while sparing FGFR1.

units.title: The disease
units.text: Cancers driven by FGFR alterations: FGFR3 in bladder cancer, FGFR2 in cholangiocarcinoma, gastric and uterine cancer. Three pan-FGFR inhibitors are approved, and patients on them relapse.

units.title: The selectivity problem
units.text: Two selectivity problems at once. Inhibiting FGFR1 is thought to cause the hyperphosphataemia that is the commonest toxicity of the approved drugs, so FGFR1 had to be spared by more than 20-fold. And resistance arises from gatekeeper mutations (FGFR3 V555I/L/M/F, FGFR2 V564I/L/M/F) whose larger residue can no longer accommodate the 3,5-dimethoxyphenyl group the approved drugs bind through, so a chemotype was needed that does not rely on that pocket at all.

units.title: The property problem
units.text: CYP3A4 inhibition and cell permeability, which moved against each other: the polar core that cleared CYP3A4 would not cross a membrane, and the permeable core inhibited CYP3A4.

units.title: Hit FGFR1 and the phosphate goes up; miss the mutants and the cancer comes back
units.text: Three pan-FGFR inhibitors are approved, and Table 9 shows what is wrong with them. All three are as potent on FGFR1 as on the target isoforms, and FGFR1 inhibition is the hypothesised cause of the hyperphosphataemia that is their commonest toxicity. All three also collapse on the gatekeeper mutants that drive clinical resistance: erdafitinib loses 35-fold on FGFR3 V555L, pemigatinib 220-fold. They bind through a 3,5-dimethoxyphenyl group that reaches past the gatekeeper, and a larger gatekeeper residue leaves it nowhere to go. A different chemotype was needed, not a better version of the same one.

units.title: Hit FGFR1 and the phosphate goes up; miss the mutants and the cancer comes back
units.text: Three drugs of this kind are already approved, and both of their weaknesses come from the same place. They block a related protein they should leave alone, which raises phosphate in the blood. And when the target protein mutates, in the exact spot these drugs reach into, they stop working and the cancer returns. Both problems trace to one part of the molecule, so the answer was not a better version of it: it was a different sort of molecule.

units.title: One carbon too many, then a branch that fitted
units.text: The screening hit 4 was already unusual: 68 nM on FGFR3 and 22 nM on the V555L mutant, so mutant tolerance came free with the chemotype. A methoxy at the ether vector took potency to 4.6 nM. Growing it to ethoxy then cost four-fold, which normally means the pocket is full. The informative result is compound 9: the bulkier but branched isopropoxy lost nothing at all. A pocket that rejects a linear group and accepts a branched one is not small, it is shaped, and that is what suggested a ring would fit.

units.title: One carbon too many, then a branch that fitted
units.text: The starting compound already worked on the mutated protein, which was half the problem solved by luck. Making one group slightly bigger made things worse, which usually means there is no more room. But a bigger, branched group worked perfectly well. That combination says the space is not too small, it is a particular shape, and the way to use it is a ring.

units.title: A hydrogen bond drawn before it existed
units.text: Docking compound 9 into FGFR3 put the isopropyl group beside Asn562, and the design became explicit: deliver a heteroatom there and engage the asparagine N-H. The oxetane 16 gave 1.1 nM, fifty-fold better, with FGFR1 selectivity up to 65-fold. Resolving the tetrahydrofuran settled the rest: the (S) enantiomer 19 is 0.9 nM and the (R) enantiomer 41 nM, a 45-fold difference between mirror images. The authors note honestly that FGFR1 carries the same asparagine, so modelling did not explain why selectivity improved too.

units.title: A hydrogen bond drawn before it existed
units.text: A computer model suggested that an oxygen atom, placed just so, could grab a specific part of the protein. Building that molecule made it fifty times more potent, which is about as good as structure-based design gets. Splitting it into its two mirror-image forms showed one does nearly all the work. The chemists also say plainly that their model could not explain the selectivity that came with it.

units.title: The ring was the wrong way round, and that explained the mutants
units.text: The co-crystal structure of compound 30 in FGFR2 at 2.68 A confirmed the designed contact: the tetrahydrofuran oxygen does hydrogen bond the asparagine, Asn571 here and Asn562 in FGFR3. Everything else about the pose was wrong. The pyridyl ring sits flipped relative to the model, with the amide reaching into the sugar pocket and the pyridine nitrogen pointing at the gatekeeper. That misplacement is the explanation for the one weakness of the lead: a polar nitrogen against the larger, more lipophilic V555L and V555M gatekeepers, and five to ten-fold potency lost.

units.title: The ring was the wrong way round, and that explained the mutants
units.text: The crystal structure showed the designed contact was real. It also showed that a whole ring of the molecule sits the opposite way round to what the model predicted, pointing a polar atom straight at the part of the protein that mutates. That single misunderstanding explains why the final compound, unlike its predecessors, loses some potency against the mutated forms. Being wrong in a way you can see is more useful than being vaguely right.

units.title: A rearranged core, and three heavy hydrogens
units.text: Two problems remained, and they pulled against each other: the polar core that spared CYP3A4 would not enter cells, and the permeable one inhibited it. Moving the bridgehead nitrogen to give a pyrazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidine cut the polarity and took cellular potency from 969 nM to 29 nM. The CYP3A4 liability was traced to N-demethylation of the amide, so the N-methyl became N-CD3: a carbon-deuterium bond is harder to break. Compound 29 cleared CYP3A4 past 25 uM, halved clearance, kept 0.5 nM potency, and reached 82 per cent oral bioavailability in rat with serum phosphate flat.

units.title: A rearranged core, and three heavy hydrogens
units.text: Two problems were left, and fixing one made the other worse: the version that left the liver alone could not get into cells, and the one that got into cells upset the liver. Rearranging the middle of the molecule solved the first. For the second, three hydrogens were swapped for a heavier form of hydrogen, making that part of the molecule harder for the body to pull apart. The result works in animals, and the phosphate problem that dogs the approved drugs did not appear.

units.title: A methoxy for fifteen-fold potency
units.text: Adding a methoxy group at the carbon adjacent to the pyridazine nitrogen took FGFR3 from 68 nM to 4.6 nM while holding FGFR1 selectivity at about 19-fold. This position, the ether vector, became the campaign's main potency lever and everything in Tables 2 and 3 explores it.

units.title: A methoxy for fifteen-fold potency
units.text: Adding a single small group made the compound fifteen times more potent without costing any of the selectivity it already had. That spot on the molecule turned out to be the one worth pushing on.

units.title: One carbon too many
units.text: Growing the methoxy to an ethoxy cost four-fold potency, 13 nM to 56 nM. Read alone this says the pocket is small and the campaign should stop here.

units.title: One carbon too many
units.text: Making the group one carbon bigger made the compound four times worse, which normally means there is no room. That reading turned out to be wrong.

units.title: The branch that changed the plan
units.text: The bulkier isopropoxy did not lose potency relative to ethoxy, 54 nM against 56 nM. A branched group being tolerated where a linear one was not is what told the authors that sp3 rings would fit, and it is the observation the rest of the paper is built on.

units.title: The branch that changed the plan
units.text: A bigger but branched group worked just as well as the smaller straight one. That is the clue that the pocket is not too small after all: it is a particular shape, and rings would fit it.

units.title: Cyclised onto an oxetane
units.text: Docking compound 9 into FGFR3 placed the isopropyl beside Asn562, suggesting a heteroatom there could engage the asparagine N-H. Cyclising to an oxetane gave 1.1 nM, a fifty-fold gain, and lifted FGFR1 selectivity to 65-fold.

units.title: Cyclised onto an oxetane
units.text: The computer model suggested that putting an oxygen atom in the right place would let the molecule grab a nearby part of the protein. Making that change made it fifty times more potent.

units.title: The active enantiomer
units.text: The racemic tetrahydrofuran 17 gave 2.4 nM. Resolving it showed the whole of the activity sits in one enantiomer: the (S) isomer 19 at 0.9 nM against the (R) isomer 18 at 41 nM, a 45-fold difference between mirror images. 19 was the first sub-nanomolar compound in the series.

units.title: The active enantiomer
units.text: The compound was a mixture of two mirror-image forms. Separating them showed one form does nearly all the work and its mirror image is forty-five times weaker. Nothing about the molecule changed except which hand it was.

units.title: Fluorine para to the amide kills two off-targets
units.text: A fluorine para to the N-methyl amide abolished KIT and PDGFRB activity: KIT 33 nM to 180 nM and PDGFRB 38 nM to 348 nM, with FGFR3 potency roughly held.

units.title: Fluorine para to the amide kills two off-targets
units.text: One fluorine atom in the right place stopped the compound hitting two unrelated proteins it should not have been touching.

units.title: A methyl meta to the amide clears the other two
units.text: A methyl in the meta position cut FLT3 and TRKA: FLT3 25 nM to 114 nM and TRKA 118 nM to 363 nM. With the R4 fluorine handling KIT and PDGFRB, the two trends together define the substitution pattern the lead needs.

units.title: A methyl meta to the amide clears the other two
units.text: A methyl group in a different position dealt with the other two unwanted targets. Put both changes on the same molecule and all four problems go at once.

units.title: Both trends on one ring
units.text: Combining the meta methyl with the para fluorine gave compound 23 at 0.7 nM with more than 100-fold selectivity over all four problem kinases: KIT 1657 nM and PDGFRB 1386 nM.

units.title: Both trends on one ring
units.text: Putting both fixes on the same molecule worked exactly as predicted, which is rarer than it sounds. The result is potent and leaves the other four proteins alone.

units.title: Methyl to fluorine for the best profile
units.text: Replacing the meta methyl with fluorine gave the best biochemical potency of the series at 0.6 nM with the cleanest kinase profile, cellular potency of 6.8 nM, low clearance and good solubility. It also inhibited CYP3A4 at 3.9 uM, which is what sent the campaign back to compound 20.

units.title: Methyl to fluorine for the best profile
units.text: This version was the best of the series on every measure the chemists had been optimising, and then failed on one they had not: it blocked a liver enzyme that drugs must leave alone.

units.title: Moving the bridgehead nitrogen
units.text: Switching the imidazo[1,2-b]pyridazine core to a pyrazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidine makes a much less basic, less polar bicycle. FGFR3 potency doubled to 1.0 nM and cellular potency improved from 969 nM to 29 nM: a 33-fold gain in translation from enzyme to cell, with CYP3A4 still clean.

units.title: Moving the bridgehead nitrogen
units.text: Rearranging the core of the molecule, so one nitrogen sits in a different place, made it far better at getting into cells. The same compound went from barely working in cells to working thirty times better.

units.title: Isopropyl for permeability
units.text: Replacing the pyrazole N-methyl with isopropyl raised Caco-2 permeability from 0.2 to 1.5 and gave 0.4 nM potency with 7.2 nM in cells. CYP3A4 inhibition remained at 9 uM.

units.title: Isopropyl for permeability
units.text: A slightly larger group on one ring helped the compound cross the gut wall, and made it more potent at the same time. The liver enzyme problem was still there.

units.title: Three deuteriums to close a metabolic door
units.text: If CYP3A4 inhibition came from the amide carbonyl or its N-demethylated metabolite, blocking N-demethylation should remove it. The N-CD3 congener cleared CYP3A4 past 25 uM and halved intrinsic clearance from 1.0 to 0.5 L/h/kg while keeping potency at 0.5 nM. The N-ethyl analogue 28 cleared CYP3A4 too, but lost potency and selectivity, so the deuterium is doing something the extra carbon cannot.

units.title: Three deuteriums to close a metabolic door
units.text: Replacing three ordinary hydrogens with their heavier isotope makes one bond harder to break, so the body cannot strip that group off as easily. The liver enzyme problem disappeared, the compound lasted longer, and its potency was untouched.

units.title: The alternative that did not work
units.text: Increasing the amide's steric bulk with an N-ethyl group also cleared CYP3A4 past 25 uM, but potency fell to 2.6 nM and FGFR1 selectivity to 21-fold. It is the control that shows the deuterium in 29 is not simply bulk.

units.title: The alternative that did not work
units.text: Making the same group bigger, rather than heavier, also fixed the liver problem but made the compound worse at its job. It is the comparison that proves the heavier-hydrogen trick was the right one.

units.title: 8E1X, FGFR2
units.text: Compound 30 in the FGFR2 kinase domain at 2.68 A. FGFR2 crystallised more readily than FGFR3 and compound 30 is equipotent in both, so this is the structure the design was checked against. The tetrahydrofuran oxygen makes the designed hydrogen bond to Asn571 (Asn562 in FGFR3 numbering). The pyridyl ring, however, is flipped relative to the docking model: the pyridine nitrogen points at the gatekeeper Val564 (Val555 in FGFR3), which is what explains the potency lost on the V555L and V555M mutants.

units.title: 8E1X, FGFR2
units.text: The compound sitting in its target protein. One contact here was designed on a computer beforehand and turned out to be right. Another part of the molecule sits the opposite way round to what was predicted, and that mistake is what explains why the drug works less well on the mutated forms of the protein.

units.title: 4K33, FGFR3
units.text: The FGFR3 kinase domain used for the docking in Figure 2, which produced the design hypothesis that an sp3 ring at the ether could reach Asn562. The paper calls it apo FGFR3; the deposited entry is in fact the K650E gain-of-function mutant with AMP-PCP and magnesium bound. It is shown here as the reference structure the model was built on, not as a structure of any compound in this campaign.

units.title: 4K33, FGFR3
units.text: The protein used for the computer model that suggested the key design change. No compound from this paper is in it: it is the starting picture the chemists reasoned from, and the real crystal structure later corrected part of that reasoning.

units.text: BUILD_SPEC 9.5 item 3: FASSIF against FaSSIF. Confirmed. Table 5 prints `FASSIF`, Table 7 prints `FaSSIF`. One assay, two spellings. The assay id is normalised to `fassif_solubility` and each source string stays in the table file it came from.

units.title: Which compound is in 8E1X, and it is not compound 29
units.text: Which compound is in 8E1X, and it is not compound 29. The RCSB entry title reads "FGFR2 kinase domain in complex with a Pyrazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidine analog (Compound 29)", while the paper's Figure 3 caption and text both say compound **30**, "an analogous compound". The coordinates settle it: the deposited ligand `U9P` is *N*-methyl-5-{5-{[(3S)-oxolan-3-yl]amino}-6-[1-(propan-2-yl)-1H-pyrazol-3-yl]pyrazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-3-yl}pyridine-3-carboxamide, which computes to **C23H26N8O2**. Compound 30's published HRMS is (M+H) C23H24D3N8O2, whose non-deuterated equivalent is exactly C23H26N8O2. Compound 29, by contrast, is C23H23D3N7O3: seven nitrogens and three oxygens, because its tetrahydrofuran is an **ether**, not an **amine**. The ligand therefore is compound 30 and the entry title is loose. The bundle records the ligand as compound 30 and the app states this on the structure caption.

units.title: Compound 30 differs from the lead in three ways at once
units.text: Compound 30 differs from the lead in three ways at once , which is why the paper calls it analogous rather than identical: the pyrazole is attached at the 3-position rather than the 4-position, the tetrahydrofuran is joined through nitrogen rather than oxygen, and the amide is N-CD3. Anyone reading the crystal structure as though it were the lead compound would be reading three edits too far along the campaign.

units.title: Deuterium is not in the deposited model
units.text: Deuterium is not in the deposited model. Compound 30 is an N-CD3 amide, and `U9P` is defined with ordinary hydrogens. X-ray structures at this resolution do not model hydrogen positions at all, so this is expected and is not a discrepancy: the depiction shown in the app is drawn from the paper's structure, with the deuterium, and the structure viewer shows the deposited coordinates.

units.title: How each structure in this bundle is verified, and how strongly
units.text: How each structure in this bundle is verified, and how strongly. The paper names only four final compounds in its Experimental Section (25, 27, 29, 30), so the other twenty-three are built by substitution on a shared core. That makes the core the thing that has to be right, and both cores are verified independently: | Core | Used by | Verified against | |---|---|---| | imidazo[1,2-b]pyridazine | 4-25 | OPSIN's parse of compound 25's published name, atom for atom | | pyrazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidine | 26-30 | OPSIN's parse of compound 27's name, **and** the deposited ligand U9P for compound 30 | Compounds 25, 27, 29 and 30 additionally match their published HRMS formulas, deuterium included. The remaining compounds rest on a verified core plus a substituent read from the table image, and are marked in `compounds.tsv` as core-verified rather than name-verified. **A formula check on its own would not have been enough.** The first version of this core reproduced compound 25's published molecular formula exactly while having the wrong connectivity: in a SMILES prefix fragment the bond to the next atom comes from the fragment's last atom, so every cyclic ether had attached through a ring carbon with its oxygen left dangling. Same atoms, wrong molecule, identical formula. Only the name-to-structure comparison caught it.

units.title: Compound 26 has no formula in the main text
units.text: Compound 26 has no formula in the main text. Its HRMS is in the Supporting Information, which is not part of this curation, so 26 is core-verified only. ## Dual residue numbering: handled, not hidden

units.title: This paper carries two numbering schemes and moves between them without warning
units.text: This paper carries two numbering schemes and moves between them without warning. The docking model and all the design discussion are in **FGFR3** numbering; the crystal structure is **FGFR2**, because FGFR2 crystallised more readily and compound 30 was confirmed equipotent in both. The equivalences are: | Role | FGFR3 | FGFR2 (in 8E1X) | |---|---|---| | Hinge | Ala558 | Ala567 | | Catalytic lysine | Lys508 | Lys517 | | Gatekeeper | Val555 | Val564 | | Lower hinge asparagine, the designed hydrogen bond | Asn562 | Asn571 | `residues.csv` is in the deposited FGFR2 numbering, because that is what the coordinates say. The FGFR3 equivalent is carried in `role_note` for each of these residues so both appear in the app, which is what BUILD_SPEC 9.2 asks for: handle it, do not hide it. ## Blanks that are real

units.text: Table 4 has genuinely empty cells , not missing transcription: compound 20 has no R3 value because its amide ring is a pyridine rather than a substituted benzene, and the V555L and V555M columns are empty for compounds 20, 5, 21 and 23. Those stay empty, and the R-group grid draws them as deliberately empty.

units.title: Compound 5 appears in three tables
units.text: Compound 5 appears in three tables (1, 2 as compound 6's benzamide counterpart, and 4) with consistent values, so it is a single row in `compounds.csv` with measurements from each table carrying their own `source_table`. ## Worth knowing when reading the story

units.title: The docking model was wrong about the pose and right about the hydrogen bond
units.text: The docking model was wrong about the pose and right about the hydrogen bond. Figure 2's model of compound 9 in FGFR3 (built on apo 4K33) predicted the amide reaching the gatekeeper. The crystal structure shows the pyridyl ring flipped, with the pyridine nitrogen pointing at the gatekeeper instead, which is what explains the V555L and V555M potency losses that the lead does show. The designed contact to the asparagine is confirmed. Both the prediction and the correction are part of the story and the app shows them as such.

units.title: 4K33 is not an apo wild-type structure
units.text: 4K33 is not an apo wild-type structure. The paper describes it as "apo FGFR3" for the docking, but the entry is the FGFR3 kinase domain carrying the **K650E** gain-of-function mutation, with AMP-PCP and magnesium bound. It is recorded as `source: referenced` with this noted, and it is not rendered as though it were the campaign's own structure.

units.title: The authors say plainly that modelling failed to explain the FGFR1 selectivity
units.text: The authors say plainly that modelling failed to explain the FGFR1 selectivity , twice: once for the amide, once for compound 19 against compound 5, since FGFR1 has the same asparagine (Asn571). They offer a subtle P-loop or backbone conformational difference as a possibility. The app must carry that as the authors' hypothesis, not as an explanation.

units.title: Discovery of INCB159020, an Orally Bioavailable KRAS G12D Inhibitor
units.text: Aspartate is not cysteine, so the covalent trick that beat KRAS G12C does not work here. This one binds without a warhead.

units.title: The disease
units.text: Cancers driven by KRAS G12D, the most common KRAS mutation: 37 per cent of pancreatic tumours and 12 per cent of colorectal. KRAS mutations drive around a fifth of all human tumours.

units.title: The selectivity problem
units.text: The mutant differs from the wild-type protein by one residue, and that residue is an aspartate rather than the cysteine that made the G12C drugs possible. Aspartate is a far weaker nucleophile, so a covalent warhead is uncertain and would need an electrophilicity that raises its own safety questions. The inhibitor therefore has to be reversible, and it still has to tell a mutant apart from a wild-type protein present in every healthy cell.

units.title: The property problem
units.text: Every substituent that bought potency also made the molecule less able to reach a cell. Two basic amines, a metabolically labile naphthol and two flexible chains gave picomolar binding with no measurable permeability, high clearance and no oral exposure at all.

units.title: The trick that beat one KRAS mutant does not work on this one
units.text: KRAS G12C fell to covalent drugs: a warhead reacts with the mutant cysteine and the inhibitor never leaves. G12D is the commoner mutation, 37 per cent of pancreatic tumours, and the swap from cysteine to aspartate removes that option. Aspartate is a far weaker nucleophile, and making a warhead reactive enough to compensate raises its own selectivity and safety problems. So the inhibitor has to be reversible, and it has to distinguish a mutant from a wild-type protein present in every healthy cell. The only starting point was a patent compound with its warhead removed: 8 uM.

units.title: The trick that beat one KRAS mutant does not work on this one
units.text: An earlier KRAS drug works by permanently latching onto a sulphur atom in the mutated protein. This mutation puts a different chemical group there, one that will not react that way, and forcing the issue would make the drug dangerously indiscriminate. So the molecule has to hold on by shape alone, and it has to tell the mutated protein apart from the healthy version in every other cell. The only place to start was a compound that barely worked.

units.title: The rigid bicycle that holds an amine below the core
units.text: A screen of rigid amines found compound 3 at 671 nM, and its crystal structure at 1.35 A explains why nearly every replacement for that group failed. The azabicyclo[2.1.1]hexane orients its protonated amine directly below the plane of the core, a conformation that is otherwise hard to reach, and from there the amine hydrogen bonds Tyr96 at 2.8 A and reaches Gly10 through a bridging water. The structure also shows what is missing: no contact at all with Asp12, the residue the whole design was aimed at.

units.title: The rigid bicycle that holds an amine below the core
units.text: A small rigid cage in the molecule holds one arm at an angle it could not otherwise adopt, and from there it grips the protein in two places, one directly and one through a single water molecule. The same picture showed what was not happening: the molecule never touched the mutated residue itself. That absence is what the chemists worked on next.

units.title: Fifty-five-fold selectivity without ever touching the mutation
units.text: Growing a two-carbon linker from the imidazole 2-position towards Asp12 gave a fifty-fold potency gain, and the structure of 5a shows why it worked and how. The amide carbonyl hydrogen bonds the backbone N-H beside Asp12, not the aspartate side chain, and that is enough for 55-fold selectivity over wild-type KRAS. Two other predictions failed in the same structure: the switch II loop did not open into an extended pocket, and the cyanoethyl intended to prise it open had instead folded under the core onto the same water as the bicyclic amine.

units.title: Fifty-five-fold selectivity without ever touching the mutation
units.text: The molecule now reaches the mutated residue, but not in the way anyone expected. It grips the protein's backbone just beside the mutation rather than the mutated part itself, and that alone is enough to prefer the mutant over the healthy protein fifty-five times over. Two other predictions in the same picture turned out wrong, which is a normal day in this work.

units.title: The best binder in the programme could not leave the gut
units.text: Compound 10 bottomed out the binding assay below 1 pM and was a dead end: no measurable Caco-2 flux at all, clearance above 1.1 L/h/kg, four identified liabilities and every one of them worth more than ten-fold of potency. Removing any single liability cost 200-fold; removing two cost thirty-fold more again. A 1 us molecular dynamics run settled where to spend the next effort: the cyanoethyl already sits mostly in its bioactive conformation, while the ethyl amide samples a wide ensemble of which the useful shape is a small sliver. Locking that amide into a ring is what broke the deadlock.

units.title: The best binder in the programme could not leave the gut
units.text: The strongest compound the team ever made was useless as a medicine: it could not cross a membrane and the liver cleared it quickly. Everything that made it potent also made it impossible to absorb, and removing any one of those features cost most of the potency. A simulation of the molecule's movement showed which flexible arm to tie down, and tying it down is what let the rest of the work proceed.

units.title: A thousand-fold weaker, and the first one that works by mouth
units.text: Compound 23, INCB159020, binds around a thousand-fold more weakly than compound 10 and is the candidate. The (R)-methyl on the morpholinone linker bought five-fold in whole blood, a pyrazine for a pyridine bought two-fold more, and exchanging the fluoronaphthyl for 2-methyl-3-chlorophenyl gave away six-fold of whole blood potency in return for permeability of 3.6 and clearance of 1.0 L/h/kg. Dosed orally in non-human primate at 1.5 mg/kg it reached 42 per cent bioavailability, against zero for compound 18. In an HPAC mouse model, 300 mg/kg held near-maximal pERK inhibition out to 24 hours.

units.title: A thousand-fold weaker, and the first one that works by mouth
units.text: The compound they chose grips the protein a thousand times more weakly than their best one, and it is the one that works. Each of the last few changes traded some strength for the ability to survive the journey through a body. Given by mouth to a primate, nearly half the dose reached the bloodstream, where the previous compound managed none at all, and in mice it shut down the cancer signal for a full day.

units.title: A bridge across the piperazine
units.text: The patent hit engaged Asp12 through a piperazine nitrogen. Bridging that ring took exchange potency from 8 uM to 704 nM, an observation several groups made independently. It is the first evidence that a reversible inhibitor of G12D was worth pursuing at all.

units.title: A bridge across the piperazine
units.text: The starting molecule was barely active. Adding a bridge across one of its rings, so it could no longer flex, made it ten times better. That was the first sign this approach could work without the chemical warhead that earlier drugs relied on.

units.title: A new core, and a cage that holds an amine where it should not reach
units.text: Moving to a tricyclic imidazole scaffold with an azabicyclo[2.1.1]hexane held potency at 671 nM while changing chemical series entirely. The crystal structure explains why almost every replacement for that cage failed: it orients the protonated amine directly below the plane of the core, a conformation that is otherwise hard to reach, where it hydrogen bonds Tyr96 at 2.8 A and reaches Gly10 through a bridging water.

units.title: A new core, and a cage that holds an amine where it should not reach
units.text: The chemists rebuilt the molecule around a different core, keeping a small rigid cage that holds one arm in an unusual position. The crystal structure shows that arm gripping the protein in two places. Almost nothing else they tried in that position worked, and now they could see why.

units.title: A two-carbon reach towards the mutation
units.text: The structure of 3 showed no contact with Asp12 at all, which made the imidazole 2-position an obvious vector. A two-carbon linker capped with a tertiary amide proved the right length, with shorter and longer chains both worse, and changing chloro to methyl at the 8 position added about two-fold. Together, fifty-fold: 671 nM to 12 nM, and the first cellular activity at 1.3 uM.

units.title: A two-carbon reach towards the mutation
units.text: The first crystal structure showed the molecule never touched the mutated residue it was aimed at. Adding an arm of exactly the right length to reach it made the compound fifty times more potent, and for the first time it worked in cells.

units.title: A cyanoethyl that folds back under the core
units.text: Replacing the 8-methyl with cyanoethyl took exchange potency to 2.9 nM, the floor of that assay, and SPR binding a hundred-fold beyond compound 4 to 0.02 nM. The intention was to push the switch II loop open into an extended pocket. The structure of 5a shows that is not what happened: the loop sits where it always did and the cyanoethyl has bent underneath the core to hydrogen bond the same water as the bicyclic amine.

units.title: A cyanoethyl that folds back under the core
units.text: Adding a small nitrile-tipped arm made the compound a hundred times stronger. The chemists expected it to prise open a loop of the protein. The crystal structure shows it did nothing of the kind: it tucked underneath the molecule and grabbed the same water molecule the other arm was already holding.

units.title: Imidazole to indole, for polarity
units.text: Swapping the imidazole core nitrogen for a C-H gives the indole core, reducing polarity. Potency is essentially unchanged, and cellular translation improves subtly, which was enough to carry the indole forward for all later work.

units.title: Imidazole to indole, for polarity
units.text: Changing one nitrogen atom in the core for a carbon made the molecule slightly less polar. It did not change how well it worked, but it moved a little closer to being something that could get into cells, so the chemists kept it.

units.title: The best binder the programme ever made
units.text: Replacing the amino azetidine with a fluorinated bicyclic pyrrolizidine ether, a fragment first reported by Mirati, bottomed out the SPR assay below 1 pM and gave 20 nM in cells with 410 nM in whole blood. It is also the compound that proved the approach could not continue: no measurable Caco-2 flux at all, and clearance above 1.1 L/h/kg.

units.title: The best binder the programme ever made
units.text: This was the most potent compound of the whole programme, binding so tightly the instrument could not measure it. It was also a dead end: it could not cross a cell membrane at any measurable rate, and the liver cleared it quickly. Potency was never going to be the problem again.

units.title: One liability removed: the basic amine
units.text: Replacing the pyrrolidinol with a simple ethoxy costs 200-fold of binding but holds whole blood potency within two-fold. It removes one of the two basic amines, which was the first of two hard requirements the team set itself.

units.title: One liability removed: the basic amine
units.text: Taking away one of the molecule's two strongly basic groups cost a great deal of raw binding strength but barely changed how well it worked in blood. That trade is the whole strategy of the rest of the paper.

units.title: The other liability: the naphthol
units.text: Converting the 3-hydroxynaphthol to 7-fluoronaphthyl removes a metabolic liability and a hydrogen bond donor, again at about 200-fold of binding and about two-fold of whole blood potency.

units.title: The other liability: the naphthol
units.text: The molecule carried a chemical group known to be broken down quickly by the body. Removing it cost binding strength but, again, hardly any real-world potency.

units.title: Both at once, and it breaks
units.text: Combining the two changes that each cost 200-fold separately loses more than 30-fold beyond that, and improves clearance only moderately with no gain in permeability. Removing both liabilities was necessary, and on this scaffold it was not possible.

units.title: Both at once, and it breaks
units.text: Each change on its own was affordable. Doing both to the same molecule was not: it lost far more than the two losses added together, and still would not cross a membrane. Something else had to change.

units.title: The lactam a microsecond of simulation asked for
units.text: A 1 us molecular dynamics run on the ground state showed the cyanoethyl already sits mostly in its bioactive conformation, while the ethyl amide samples a wide ensemble of which the bioactive form is a small sliver. Locking that amide into a gamma-lactam improved binding five-fold, to 0.05 nM, at the cost of whole blood potency.

units.title: The lactam a microsecond of simulation asked for
units.text: A simulation of how the molecule moves showed one arm was already held in the right shape, while another flailed around and was almost never in the useful position. Tying that arm into a ring made the compound five times stronger at binding, though not yet in blood.

units.title: Methyl restores what the lactam cost
units.text: Switching the ethoxy for a methyl recovers whole blood potency from 2354 nM to 597 nM, a trend the paper reports as consistent throughout the series.

units.title: Methyl restores what the lactam cost
units.text: Swapping one small group for an even simpler one restored most of the potency in blood that the previous change had cost.

units.title: One oxygen in the ring
units.text: Replacing the lactam's piperidinone with a morpholinone, one extra oxygen in the ring, improves cellular potency from 39 nM to 7.2 nM and whole blood from 1030 nM to 677 nM, while keeping the permeability that cyclisation first delivered.

units.title: One oxygen in the ring
units.text: Adding a single oxygen atom into one ring made the compound five times better in cells, and it kept the ability to cross membranes that the ring itself had won.

units.title: A pyridine where a basic amine used to be
units.text: With the basic amine requirement gone, the solvent position could take a heteroaryl. 2-Methylpyridin-4-yl more than doubled permeability to 1.6 and brought clearance to 1.0 L/h/kg: the first compound in the programme with both at once.

units.title: A pyridine where a basic amine used to be
units.text: Freed from needing a strongly basic group, the chemists could put a simple ring there instead. For the first time one compound both crossed membranes and survived the liver.

units.title: An (R)-methyl worth five-fold in blood
units.text: Adding a single methyl at the linker carbon, in the (R) configuration, restricts the morpholinone further and improves whole blood potency five-fold to 103 nM. Compound 21 binds a thousand times more weakly than compound 10 and is five times more potent in whole blood, which is the clearest statement of this campaign's argument.

units.title: An (R)-methyl worth five-fold in blood
units.text: One extra methyl group, in one specific three-dimensional orientation, made the compound five times more potent in blood. It binds the protein a thousand times more weakly than the programme's best binder, and works better where it matters.

units.title: Pyridine to pyrazine, less basic again
units.text: A second ring nitrogen lowers basicity: permeability more than doubles to 1.4 and whole blood potency improves again to 55 nM.

units.title: Pyridine to pyrazine, less basic again
units.text: Adding one more nitrogen to that ring made it less basic, which helped the compound cross membranes and made it twice as potent in blood.

units.title: Trading potency for a drug
units.text: Replacing the 7-fluoronaphthyl with 2-methyl-3-chlorophenyl loses six-fold of whole blood potency, from 55 nM to 331 nM. Permeability rises from 1.4 to 3.6 and clearance to 1.0 L/h/kg, and in non-human primate oral bioavailability goes from 2 per cent to 42 per cent. This is compound 23, INCB159020.

units.title: Trading potency for a drug
units.text: Swapping a large greasy ring for a smaller one made the compound six times less potent and turned it into a drug: given by mouth to a primate, forty-two per cent of the dose reached the bloodstream, against two per cent before.

units.title: 9E5F, KRAS G12D
units.text: Compound 3 bound to KRAS G12D at 1.35 A. The protonated amine of the azabicyclo[2.1.1]hexane makes two contacts: a direct hydrogen bond to Tyr96 at 2.8 A, and a water-mediated interaction reaching Gly10 at 2.9 and 3.1 A. The rigid bicycle holds that amine directly below the plane of the imidazole core, a conformation that is otherwise hard to reach, and that is why nearly every replacement for it lost potency. Note what is absent: no contact is made with Asp12, contrary to the hypothesis the compound was designed on.

units.title: 9E5F, KRAS G12D
units.text: An early compound in the pocket. A small rigid cage holds one part of the molecule in a position it would not otherwise adopt, and from there it grips the protein in two places. What the picture also shows is a missed opportunity: the molecule never reaches the mutated residue itself, which is what the chemists went after next.

units.title: 9E5D, KRAS G12D
units.text: Compound 5a, the methyl ester analogue of compound 5, bound to KRAS G12D at 1.36 A. Two hypotheses are tested here and one survives. The switch II loop did not open into an extended pocket: it sits in virtually the same conformation as in the structure of 3, and the cyanoethyl group has instead bent underneath the core to hydrogen bond the same water as the bicyclic amine. Growing from the imidazole 2-position did work: the carbonyl hydrogen bonds the backbone N-H of Asp12, and this compound holds 55-fold selectivity over wild-type KRAS without ever touching the Asp12 side chain.

units.title: 9E5D, KRAS G12D
units.text: A later compound in the same pocket. The chemists expected a loop of the protein to swing open and make room; it did not. What did work was reaching towards the mutated residue: the molecule grips the protein's backbone right beside it. That grip is enough to tell the mutant apart from the healthy version fifty-five times over, without ever touching the mutated part itself.

units.title: PLIP confirms the paper's structural argument independently
units.text: PLIP confirms the paper's structural argument independently. In 9E5F it finds the Tyr96 hydrogen bonds and a water bridge to Gly10, exactly as described. In 9E5D it finds a direct hydrogen bond to Asp12 at 1.92 A, which is the backbone contact the 55-fold wild-type selectivity is attributed to. It also finds contacts the paper does not discuss, including Glu62, Glu63 and Arg102: those are shown as measured, without being given a significance the paper never claimed for them.

units.title: Every compound in this paper is atropisomeric
units.text: Every compound in this paper is atropisomeric. Compounds 14, 18, 19 and 20 are published as mixtures of atropisomers and are flagged in the table files.
